This change was introduced in release 4.1. Source: Django 4.1 release notes (official_release_notes). Section: Django 4.1 release notes / Backwards incompatible changes in 4.1 / Admin changelist searches spanning multi-valued relationships changes.

 }

ITEM:
<<<
Admin changelist searches using multiple search terms are now applied in a single call to filter(), rather than in sequential filter() calls. For multi-valued relationships, this means that rows from the related model must match all terms rather than any term. For example, if search_fields is set to ['childname', 'childage'], and a user searches for 'Jamal 17', parent rows will be returned only if there is a relationship to some 17-year-old child named Jamal, rather than also returning parents who merely have a younger or older child named Jamal in addition to some other 17-year-old. See the spanning-multi-valued-relationships topic for more discussion of this difference. In Django 4.0 and earlier, get_search_results followed the second example query, but this undocumented behavior led to queries with excessive joins.
>>>

paths.path_name: Admin multi-term search over multi-valued relationships now requires all terms to match the same related row
paths.description: Since Django 4.1, admin changelist searches with multiple search terms are applied in a single filter() call. For search_fields spanning multi-valued relationships, a single related row must now match all terms, so searches that previously returned parents matching terms via different related rows now return fewer results.

conditions.statement: The upgrade crosses Django 4.1, where admin multi-term search behavior changed (3.2 -> 4.2 includes 4.1).
quotes: Admin changelist searches using multiple search terms are now applied in a single call to filter(), rather than in sequential filter() calls.
conditions.relevance: Ties the behavior change to the 4.1 release, which is crossed when upgrading from 3.2 to 4.2.

conditions.statement: A ModelAdmin defines search_fields that span a multi-valued relationship (e.g. reverse foreign key or many-to-many), such as ['childname', 'childage'].
quotes: For multi-valued relationships, this means that rows from the related model must match all terms rather than any term.
conditions.relevance: The changed semantics only affect searches over multi-valued relationships.
ambiguities: The text does not state how to determine which search_fields entries span multi-valued relationships; this requires inspecting model relations.

conditions.statement: The application overrides or calls get_search_results, which followed the old sequential-filter behavior in 4.0 and earlier.
quotes: In Django 4.0 and earlier, get_search_results followed the second example query
conditions.relevance: Custom overrides of get_search_results may depend on or interact with the previous behavior.
ambiguities: The text does not say whether custom overrides of get_search_results are affected.

conditions.statement: Users or tests rely on multi-term admin searches returning parents whose different related rows each match different terms.
quotes: parent rows will be returned only if there is a relationship to some 17-year-old child named Jamal
conditions.relevance: Such searches return fewer rows after the upgrade.
ambiguities: The text does not state whether any given application relies on the old matching behavior.

suggested_actions: Review ModelAdmin.search_fields entries that span multi-valued relationships and confirm that requiring a single related row to match all search terms is acceptable.
Review any get_search_results overrides and tests of admin search results for dependence on the previous behavior.
See the spanning-multi-valued-relationships topic in the Django documentation for a discussion of the difference between the two query forms.
